stories.title: The Ancient Manuscript
stories.description: Amit and Ajay start the episode with a prop—a 'leaf' or ancient manuscript—to playfully introduce the topic of populism and the importance of understanding technical terms correctly.

stories.title: Ajay's 'Clueless Economist' Moment
stories.description: Ajay admits that for years he thought 'populism' just meant 'popular' and couldn't understand why it was considered bad, until he learned the specific political science definition involving anti-pluralism and anti-elitism.

stories.title: Jeff Bezos vs. Trump
stories.description: Ajay recounts how Jeff Bezos, despite having the most to lose as a rich man, stood up to Donald Trump. Trump tried to weaponize the IRS and FBI against him, but the institutions refused, highlighting the strength of the US system.

stories.title: Israel's Judicial Protests
stories.description: The story of how Israeli society, including elite military reservists, mobilized to protest against Netanyahu's attempt to undermine the judiciary, showing the liberal core of the country.

stories.title: Poland's Redemption
stories.description: Ajay tells the story of Poland: from being crushed by Nazis and Soviets, to rising after 1989, falling back into populism under the Law and Justice party, and finally redeeming itself with the recent election of Donald Tusk.

stories.title: Beauty and the Beast
stories.description: Ajay uses the scene where Gaston dismisses Belle's book because it has 'no pictures' to mock the 'WhatsApp university' culture where people can't process complex text-based arguments.

core_ideas.description: Populism is not just being popular. It is a specific political logic that claims only some people are 'the real people', rejects pluralism, and attacks elites and institutions.

Populists use a standard toolkit: defining the 'real' people, anti-elite rhetoric, victimhood narratives, monolithic parties, fake proximity to the people, simplistic narratives, and conspiracy theories.
Once in power, populists try to take over independent institutions (courts, media, central banks) and fill them with loyalists to consolidate control.
Populist regimes use state resources for 'bread and circuses'—subsidies and spectacles—to buy loyalty and distract the population.
Populists don't need to jail everyone; they just need to make examples of a few dissenters to create a climate of fear where civil society self-censors.
A true democracy requires more than just accurate vote counting. It needs a level playing field: free media, freedom to campaign, independent funding, and safety from state harassment.
Ajay argues that cultural, business, and intellectual elites drive progress and truth. Attacking them is a destructive populist tactic that leads to mediocrity.
